abstract: Upgrades an existing Gradle wrapper to a target version on Gradle 7.0 through 9.x, in six steps: read the current version and distribution type from gradle-wrapper.properties; resolve the target version (the latest release when the user names none) and look up that distribution's published SHA-256; run the tasks task to record a baseline and secure the four wrapper files, using a clean git worktree where there is one and a copy outside the project tree otherwise; run the built-in wrapper task twice with the version and checksum pinned; verify by diff and re-run the tasks canary; and roll back if the build no longer configures. Running the task twice is the point most upgrades get wrong — the first run rewrites gradlew, gradlew.bat and gradle-wrapper.jar from the old version's templates and only the second regenerates them from the new one — and verification is by diff rather than by version string, because a half-done upgrade still reports the new version. The canary exists to catch the dangerous case: an upgrade whose four files all land correctly but leaves a build that no longer configures is a failed job, not a successful one, and is rolled back rather than reported as done. Two reference files carry branches most upgrades never reach and are opened only when their case arises — one for snapshotting and restoring the wrapper where git cannot, one for the rollback procedure and the report that must follow it, which states plainly that the upgrade did not happen, quotes the failure, recommends a smaller intermediate version without performing it, and links that version's release notes and, for a major, its upgrade guide. Along the way it explains why the canary is tasks rather than build and what configuration-on-demand does to that choice, why a snapshot must cover the scripts and jar rather than the properties alone, how to pick the right checksum among those published per release, the rules that apply once distributionSha256Sum is set, the labels accepted by --gradle-version, and the Gradle 9 requirement that gradle-wrapper.properties declare a full X.Y.Z version. It distinguishes 'upgrade it' (execute the steps) from 'how do I upgrade' (hand over the commands), and draws its rollback line at the build phase rather than the command: a build that no longer configures is rolled back, while an execution-phase failure such as a compile error or a failing test is left in place and reported. Deliberately narrow — it does not add a wrapper to a project that has none, configure authenticated distributions, customize the Wrapper task, or repair a build in either direction, neither to force a blocked upgrade through nor to fix what the new version broke.
